title: Kidney Pain After Drinking: Flank vs. Back Pain and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your kidneys can ache after drinking, how to tell kidney pain from back pain, the causes behind beer-triggered and one-sided pain, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Kidney pain after drinking alcohol? How to tell flank pain from back pain, why beer can trigger it, what to do at home, and signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** an ache in your kidney area after a night of drinking is usually your body telling you it's low on fluid. Alcohol makes you pee out more water than you take in, and the dull, both-sided ache that some people feel under their back ribs the next morning tends to fade once they rehydrate. Many "kidney" pains after drinking also turn out to be plain back muscles. But a few causes are worth taking seriously: kidney stones (our guide on whether [alcohol causes kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones) covers the link), kidney infections, a drainage problem that shows up only when you drink a lot of fluid quickly, and, rarely, sudden kidney injury after a heavy binge. This guide shows you how to tell kidney pain from back pain, what each cause feels like, what to do at home, and which signs mean you should see a doctor.

**The quick rules:** Kidney pain sits higher and more to the side than most back pain, just under the lower ribs. A mild, dull ache on both sides that eases with water, food, and rest is usually dehydration. Sharp pain on one side, pain with fever, blood in your urine, or pain that comes back every time you drink is not a hangover symptom, and it needs a doctor. Go easy on ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers while you're dehydrated, because they make the kidneys' job harder.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have** severe pain that makes it hard to sit still, flank pain with a high fever and shaking chills, vomiting so persistent you can't keep water down, little or no urine for many hours, confusion or trouble staying awake, or urine that's dark brown or cola-colored along with severe muscle pain or weakness. **See a doctor the same day if** you have flank pain with fever, burning when you pee, or blood in your urine, or sharp one-sided pain that comes in waves and spreads toward your groin. **Book a regular appointment if** the same pain shows up every time you drink, it lasts more than a couple of days, or you have known kidney disease, diabetes, or high blood pressure. If you're pregnant, any flank pain with fever needs prompt care.

## Is It Your Kidneys or Your Back? Flank Pain vs. Back Pain

Most people picture their kidneys low in the back, near the belt line. They actually sit higher than that. Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs tucked against the back wall of your abdomen, on either side of your spine, mostly behind your lowest ribs. The right one sits a little lower than the left because the liver is above it.

That's why doctors talk about **flank pain** when they suspect a kidney problem. The flank is the area on your side, between the bottom of your rib cage and the top of your hip bone, toward the back. If you put your hands on your hips with your thumbs pointing backward, your thumbs are roughly below where your kidneys sit.

Here's how the two kinds of pain usually differ:

| | Kidney pain | Back muscle pain |
|---|---|---|
| **Where** | High, under the back ribs, toward the side | Usually lower, across the low back or along the spine |
| **Sides** | Often one side (stones, infection); dehydration can cause a mild ache on both | Either or both sides, often across the middle |
| **Feel** | Deep, dull ache, or sharp waves (stones) | Sore, tight, stiff, or achy |
| **Movement** | Doesn't change much when you move, stretch, or change position | Gets worse with certain movements, better with others |
| **Touch** | Tapping gently over the area can hurt (doctors check this) | A sore spot you can press on in the muscle |
| **Spreads to** | Sometimes the lower belly, groin, or inner thigh | Sometimes the buttock or down the leg |
| **Comes with** | Changes in urine, fever, nausea | Stiffness, sore muscles elsewhere |

A useful self-check: if the pain gets clearly worse when you bend, twist, or press on a specific muscle, and better when you lie a certain way, it's probably muscle. If it's a deep ache that stays the same no matter what position you're in, or it comes with changes in your urine, think kidneys.

If your pain is lower and changes with movement, our guide to [back pain after drinking](/never-hungover/back-pain-after-drinking) covers the muscle causes, plus the upper-back pain that can point to pancreatitis.

## What Alcohol Actually Does to Your Kidneys

Your kidneys filter your blood, balance the water and salt in your body, and decide how much fluid leaves as urine. Alcohol interferes with that last job in a direct way.

Normally your brain releases a hormone called **vasopressin** (also called antidiuretic hormone, or ADH). It tells your kidneys to hold onto water instead of sending it to your bladder. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, so your kidneys let more water through. That's why you pee so much more than you drank while you're out, and why the effect is strongest while your blood alcohol is rising. We explain the full story in [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee).

Several things follow from that:

- **You lose water and electrolytes.** Sodium, potassium, and magnesium go out with the extra urine. By morning, many people are mildly dehydrated, which is part of why hangovers bring headaches, thirst, and fatigue.
- **Your urine gets concentrated the next day.** Once the alcohol wears off, your body swings the other way and holds onto water. Your urine turns darker and more concentrated, which is one of the conditions that favors kidney stones.
- **Blood flow to the kidneys can drop if you're very dehydrated.** In a healthy person after a normal night out, the kidneys handle this without trouble. After a severe binge with vomiting and little water, the strain is real.

Your kidneys don't break down much alcohol themselves; that's mostly the liver's job. A small amount of alcohol does leave the body unchanged in urine and breath, but the kidneys' main involvement is managing the fluid shifts alcohol causes.

## Why Your Kidneys Hurt After Drinking: The Main Causes

### 1. Dehydration (the most common reason)

A dull, mild ache on both sides of your back, under the ribs, the morning after drinking, along with thirst, dark urine, a headache, and fatigue, is most often dehydration. It's uncomfortable, but for a healthy person it's usually temporary. The ache typically improves within hours of drinking water, eating, and resting.

Dehydration-related discomfort shouldn't be sharp, shouldn't sit only on one side, and shouldn't come with fever. If it does, look further down this list. You can read more about how alcohol dries you out in our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 2. Kidney stones

Kidney stones are hard clumps of minerals that form in the kidney. Many sit there for years without causing symptoms. The pain starts when a stone moves into the narrow tube (the ureter) that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder and partly blocks it.

**How it feels:** sudden, severe pain on one side of the back or flank, often coming in waves that build and ease. It can move toward the lower belly, groin, or inner thigh as the stone travels. People often can't find a comfortable position and pace around. Nausea and vomiting are common. You may see pink, red, or brown urine, or feel like you need to pee urgently and often.

**How alcohol fits in:** alcohol doesn't directly create stones, and the research is mixed in an interesting way. Some large observational studies have actually linked moderate beer and wine drinking with a lower risk of stones, probably because of the extra fluid. But a heavy night followed by a dehydrated morning concentrates your urine, which helps stone-forming minerals clump. Beer also contains purines, which the body turns into uric acid, and high uric acid is a factor in one type of stone (and in gout). The practical takeaway: drinking doesn't cause stones, but dehydration after drinking can be the moment a stone you already have starts to cause trouble, or makes new ones more likely over time.

Stone pain needs a doctor, even if it eases. Most small stones pass on their own with fluids and pain relief, but a doctor needs to confirm the size and make sure there's no infection behind the blockage. **A stone with fever is an emergency**, because an infected, blocked kidney can make you very sick quickly.

### 3. A kidney or urinary infection

Alcohol doesn't cause urinary infections. But drinking can hide the early symptoms of a bladder infection (you're peeing a lot anyway, and you're not paying attention), and dehydration means less flushing of the urinary tract. If a bladder infection travels up to the kidney, it becomes a kidney infection, which is more serious.

**Signs of a kidney infection:** flank pain, usually on one side; fever and chills; burning or pain when you pee; needing to pee often or urgently; cloudy, bad-smelling, or bloody urine; nausea or vomiting. You may feel generally unwell in a way that seems worse than a hangover and doesn't improve as the day goes on.

A kidney infection needs antibiotics, usually started the same day. Don't wait it out to see if it's "just the hangover." If you're prescribed antibiotics, ask your pharmacist about alcohol, because a few of the common ones have specific warnings.

### 4. Pain that only shows up when you drink a lot, quickly: a kidney drainage problem

Some people get the same one-sided flank pain every time they drink a large volume of fluid quickly, and beer is the classic trigger. This pattern can be a sign of a narrowing where the kidney drains into the ureter, called a **ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction**. Many people with a mild narrowing never know it's there. When alcohol suppresses vasopressin and you're also drinking several pints of liquid, the kidney makes urine faster than the narrowed outlet can drain it. The kidney stretches, and that stretching hurts.

**Clues that point to this:** pain on the same side each time; it starts during or soon after drinking a lot of beer (or even a lot of water or coffee); it fades over hours as the flow catches up; sometimes nausea comes with it. It's often first noticed in young adults.

This isn't dangerous in the moment for most people, but it's worth getting checked, because a long-standing blockage can slowly affect the kidney. An ultrasound or other imaging can show it, and it's treatable. If this description sounds familiar, tell your doctor exactly what happens and when.

### 5. Sudden kidney strain after a heavy binge (rare)

Doctors call a sudden drop in kidney function **acute kidney injury**. It's uncommon after drinking, but it does happen, usually when several things stack up: a very heavy binge, lots of vomiting, little water, sometimes anti-inflammatory painkillers on top, and sometimes a long time lying in one position.

That last point matters because of a condition called **rhabdomyolysis**, where damaged muscle breaks down and releases a protein that can clog the kidneys. After drinking, it's most often linked to passing out and lying on a hard surface for hours, or to extreme exertion while drunk. Warning signs are severe muscle pain or weakness, swelling in a limb, and urine that turns dark brown or cola-colored. **That combination is a reason to go to the emergency room**, not to wait and rehydrate at home.

Other signs that the kidneys are struggling include peeing very little or not at all for many hours despite drinking fluids, swelling in your legs or around your eyes, and unusual drowsiness or confusion.

### 6. It's actually something else nearby

Pain in the kidney area isn't always the kidneys. Possibilities include:

- **Back muscles.** Still the most likely cause of most "kidney pain," especially if it moves with your body.
- **Pancreatitis.** Severe upper belly pain that bores straight through to the back, often with vomiting, after heavy drinking. This is an emergency.
- **Gallbladder or liver.** Pain under the right ribs that can spread to the back or right shoulder blade, sometimes after a fatty meal with drinks.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, which usually causes upper belly pain rather than back pain. Our article on [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) covers this.

## Kidney Pain After Drinking Beer

Beer comes up more often than other drinks in people's searches, and there are real reasons for that:

- **Volume.** A few pints means a lot of liquid in a short time. If you have a mild drainage narrowing (described above), that volume is what brings it out. Spirits rarely trigger it the same way, because the volume is much smaller.
- **Purines.** Beer contains more purines than wine or spirits. Purines raise uric acid, which plays a part in gout and in uric acid stones.
- **Dehydration still applies.** The water in beer doesn't fully cancel out the alcohol's effect, especially with stronger craft beers.

If beer specifically gives you the same one-sided pain every time, that's the pattern doctors want to hear about. If any drink gives you a mild ache on both sides the next morning, that's more likely dehydration.

## Left Side, Right Side, or Both?

Which side hurts can help narrow things down, though it's never a diagnosis on its own.

- **Both sides, dull and mild:** most often dehydration or back muscles.
- **One side, sharp and coming in waves:** a stone on that side is high on the list.
- **One side, with fever and urinary symptoms:** possible kidney infection.
- **One side, every time you drink a lot:** possible drainage narrowing on that side.
- **Right side, high, under the ribs:** could also be the liver or gallbladder.
- **Left side, high, or upper back with belly pain:** could also be the pancreas, especially with vomiting.

## Kidney Pain the Next Day vs. While You're Drinking

**Pain the next morning** fits dehydration, back strain from a bad night's sleep, or the moment a stone starts to move after a dehydrated night. It should improve over the day as you drink water and eat.

**Pain during or right after drinking** is less typical. If it comes on within an hour or so of drinking, especially after a lot of beer, think about the drainage problem described above. A rare symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma is pain right after drinking alcohol, though that pain is usually felt in swollen lymph nodes (neck, armpit, or groin) rather than the kidneys. Either way, pain that reliably starts when you drink is something to bring to a doctor rather than ignore.

## What to Do About Kidney Pain After Drinking

If your pain is mild, on both sides, without fever, blood in your urine, or one-sided sharp waves, these steps make sense.

### 1. Rehydrate steadily

Drink water through the day rather than forcing down a huge amount at once. Sipping a glass or so every hour or so works better than chugging. If you've been vomiting or sweating, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix helps replace the sodium and potassium you lost. Watch your urine: pale yellow and regular is the goal. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains what to look for in a drink.

### 2. Eat something

Food helps your body rebalance fluids and salts. Broth-based soup, toast, bananas, eggs, or rice are easy options if your stomach is unsettled.

### 3. Use heat for muscle-type aches

A warm shower or heating pad helps if the pain is really muscular. It won't fix a kidney problem, but it's harmless and useful for figuring out which you're dealing with. If heat and gentle movement help a lot, it was probably muscle.

### 4. Be careful with painkillers

This is where kidney pain after drinking differs from a regular hangover headache.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs)** reduce blood flow to the kidneys a little. In a well-hydrated, healthy person that's rarely a problem at the label dose. In someone who's dehydrated, it adds strain at exactly the wrong time, and these drugs also irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. If you use one, rehydrate first, take it with food, and stick to the label. Avoid them if you have kidney disease. See our page on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the kidneys but processed by the liver, which is also handling alcohol. A single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared is the usual advice for occasional drinkers. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) has the details.

If you're unsure, ask a pharmacist. They can tell you what's safest for you in a minute or two.

### 5. Skip the hair of the dog

Another drink adds more of the diuretic effect that caused the problem. It may dull how you feel for an hour, but it pushes the dehydration further.

### 6. Watch how it changes

Mild dehydration pain should get better by the afternoon or evening. If it's the same or worse after a day of good hydration, or if new symptoms appear (fever, one-sided sharp pain, blood in the urine), move to the doctor checklist below.

## When to See a Doctor About Kidney Pain After Drinking

Most next-morning aches are not dangerous. These signs are different.

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have:**

- Severe flank or belly pain that makes it hard to sit or lie still
- Flank pain with a high fever, shaking chills, or feeling faint
- Vomiting you can't stop, so you can't keep water down
- Very little or no urine for many hours despite drinking fluids
- Dark brown or cola-colored urine together with severe muscle pain, weakness, or swelling
- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or trouble staying awake
- Severe upper belly pain going through to your back, with vomiting

**See a doctor the same day if you have:**

- Flank pain with fever, burning when you pee, or cloudy or bad-smelling urine
- Blood in your urine (pink, red, or brown)
- Sharp, one-sided pain in waves, especially spreading toward the groin, even if it eases
- Flank pain while pregnant

**Book a regular appointment if:**

- The same one-sided pain shows up every time you drink a lot, especially beer
- Mild pain lasts more than a couple of days after drinking
- You've had kidney stones before and the pain feels familiar
- You have diabetes, high blood pressure, or known kidney disease
- You notice swollen glands, night sweats, or weight loss along with pain after drinking

If you notice you're drinking heavily most days and can't easily cut back, or you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, those are withdrawal signals. Withdrawal can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor before stopping suddenly. That conversation is routine for doctors and there's no judgment in it.

## Can Drinking Damage Your Kidneys Long Term?

For an occasional social drinker with healthy kidneys, there's no good evidence that a night out causes lasting kidney damage. The picture changes with regular heavy drinking:

- **Blood pressure.** Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, and high blood pressure is one of the leading causes of chronic kidney disease.
- **Liver disease.** Advanced alcohol-related liver disease can affect kidney function, because the two organs are closely linked through blood flow and fluid balance.
- **Repeated dehydration and binges.** Each severe episode is a stress, and stacking them with NSAIDs or vomiting raises the chance of sudden kidney injury.
- **Existing kidney disease.** If your kidneys already work less well, alcohol and dehydration hit harder, and some kidney medicines need care around alcohol.

National health guidance, such as from the US National Kidney Foundation, generally says moderate drinking is unlikely to harm healthy kidneys, while heavy drinking raises risk. "Moderate" in US dietary guidance means up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men. Our deeper article on [alcohol and kidney disease](/never-hungover/alcohol-kidney-disease-renal-function-impact-2025) goes through the long-term research.

If you drink regularly, a routine blood test (creatinine and eGFR) and a urine test at your next checkup will tell you how your kidneys are doing. It's quick and cheap.

## How to Prevent Kidney Pain After Drinking

Most prevention comes down to managing fluid:

1. **Alternate drinks with water.** One glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and offsets some of the fluid loss.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which softens the diuretic spike.
3. **Drink water before bed.** A glass or two before sleep, and another if you wake up, means a less dehydrated morning.
4. **Go easier on volume if beer triggers pain.** If you suspect the drainage problem, switching from several pints to a smaller amount of something else may help while you get it checked, but get it checked.
5. **Don't pre-load painkillers.** Taking ibuprofen before or during drinking to "prevent" a hangover adds kidney and stomach strain without clear benefit.
6. **Know your history.** If you've had stones, staying well hydrated is the single most useful habit, on drinking nights and every other day.

For a broader plan, see our guide to [preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Where DHM fits in

Some people add a supplement to their drinking-night routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents kidney pain, kidney stones, or kidney infections, and it doesn't replace water, food, or drinking less. It doesn't affect the vasopressin effect that drives the dehydration behind most next-morning kidney aches.

If you want to try it as one part of a broader plan, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly pure DHM tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds electrolytes and other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when. If you have kidney disease or take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before starting any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Your kidneys sit high, under the back ribs and toward the sides. Pain lower down that changes with movement is usually muscle.
- The most common reason for a kidney-area ache after drinking is dehydration, because alcohol blocks the hormone that tells your kidneys to save water. It should ease with fluids, food, and rest.
- Sharp one-sided pain in waves suggests a stone. Flank pain with fever or burning when you pee suggests an infection. Both need a doctor.
- The same one-sided pain every time you drink a lot, especially beer, can be a kidney drainage narrowing that's worth checking with imaging.
- Dark brown urine with severe muscle pain, little or no urine, confusion, or pain with high fever are emergency signs.
- Be careful with ibuprofen and other NSAIDs while dehydrated, and remember that occasional drinking is unlikely to harm healthy kidneys, while regular heavy drinking raises the long-term risk.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do my kidneys hurt after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reason is dehydration. Alcohol blocks vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose more fluid than you drink. A dull ache on both sides under your back ribs the next morning often eases once you rehydrate. Sharp one-sided pain, pain with fever, or blood in your urine points to something else, such as a kidney stone or infection, and needs a doctor.

**How do I know if it's kidney pain or back pain?**

Kidney pain sits higher and more to the side, just under the lower ribs, feels deep, and doesn't change much when you move. It can come with changes in your urine or fever. Back muscle pain is usually lower, feels sore or stiff, and gets better or worse with certain movements or positions.

**Is kidney pain after drinking serious?**

Usually not, if it's a mild ache on both sides that clears up as you rehydrate. It is serious if it comes with fever, chills, blood in the urine, vomiting you can't stop, very little urine, confusion, or dark brown urine with muscle pain. Those signs need same-day care or the emergency room.

**Why do my kidneys hurt after drinking beer specifically?**

Beer means a large volume of liquid in a short time, plus alcohol's diuretic effect. If you have a mild narrowing where the kidney drains, that flood of urine can stretch the kidney and cause one-sided pain that fades over hours. Beer is also higher in purines, which raise uric acid. If beer reliably gives you pain on the same side, mention it to a doctor, who can check with an ultrasound.

**How long does kidney pain from drinking last?**

Dehydration-related aches usually improve within hours and are gone within a day once you drink fluids and eat. Pain that lasts more than a couple of days, keeps coming back, or gets worse despite good hydration should be checked by a doctor.

**Can I take ibuprofen for kidney pain after drinking?**

Be cautious. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin reduce blood flow to the kidneys slightly, which matters more when you're dehydrated, and they irritate the stomach. If you take one, rehydrate first, eat, and stay within the label dose. Avoid them if you have kidney disease. Acetaminophen is easier on the kidneys but has its own liver considerations with alcohol. A pharmacist can help you choose.

**Can one night of drinking damage your kidneys?**

For most healthy people, no. Occasional drinking is unlikely to harm healthy kidneys. In rare cases, a very heavy binge combined with severe dehydration, vomiting, NSAIDs, or a long time lying in one position can cause sudden kidney injury. Signs include very little urine, swelling, confusion, or dark brown urine, and they need emergency care.

**Does drinking water help kidney pain after drinking?**

Yes, if the cause is dehydration, which it usually is. Sip water steadily through the day and add an electrolyte drink if you've been vomiting. If the pain doesn't improve after a day of good hydration, or new symptoms appear, see a doctor.

**Does DHM help with kidney pain after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats kidney pain, stones, or infections. Its research focuses on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animals. The best ways to prevent kidney-area aches after drinking are water between drinks, food, and drinking less. If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor before trying any supplement.
